```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
has_survival <- requireNamespace("survival", quietly = TRUE)
has_metafor <- requireNamespace("metafor", quietly = TRUE)
```

```{r}
library(adempR)
```

These examples show common study types. They use few replications so the
vignette builds quickly; a real study would plan the number with
`sim_plan_replications()` or `sim_pilot()`.

## Clustered data: ignoring the clustering

Patients are grouped in centers, and the treatment is assigned by center.
Ordinary least squares gives an unbiased treatment effect but standard
errors that are too small. A cluster-robust (sandwich) standard error, or
analysis of the cluster means, fixes this.

```{r}
clustered <- sim_study("clustered",
  scenarios = sim_scenarios(clusters = c(10L, 40L), icc = c(0.05, 0.2), m = 20L),
  generate = function(scenario, context) {
    d <- sim_rclustered(scenario$clusters, scenario$m, icc = scenario$icc)
    d$a <- as.integer(d$cluster %% 2 == 0)
    d$y <- d$y + 0.3 * d$a
    # the latent cluster effect is kept away from the methods
    sim_data(d[c("cluster", "a", "y")], meta = list(u = d$u))
  },
  estimands = list(sim_estimand("effect", effect = "marginal",
                                truth = sim_truth_exact(function(scenario) 0.3))),
  methods = list(
    ols = function(data) {
      f <- lm(y ~ a, data)
      b <- unname(coef(f)["a"]); se <- sqrt(vcov(f)["a", "a"])
      sim_estimate("effect", b, se = se, lower = b - 1.96 * se, upper = b + 1.96 * se,
                   level = 0.95)
    },
    cluster_means = function(data) {
      cm <- aggregate(y ~ cluster + a, data, mean)
      f <- lm(y ~ a, cm)
      b <- unname(coef(f)["a"]); se <- sqrt(vcov(f)["a", "a"])
      q <- qt(0.975, df.residual(f))
      sim_estimate("effect", b, se = se, lower = b - q * se, upper = b + q * se,
                   level = 0.95)
    }),
  measures = c("bias", "empse", "rmvar", "se_ratio", "coverage"))
run <- sim_run(clustered, replications = 150, seed = 1,
               path = file.path(tempdir(), "clustered"))
s <- as.data.frame(sim_summarise(run))
s[s$measure %in% c("se_ratio", "coverage"),
  c("scenario_id", "method", "measure", "value", "mcse")]
```

`sim_rclustered()` returns a cluster identifier, an outcome `y` with total
variance 1 and intraclass correlation `icc`, and the cluster effect `u`.
The generator passes `u` as protected metadata, so no method can use it.

## Survival: a risk at a fixed horizon

The estimand is the risk of an event by year 2 in the treated arm, a
scalar summary of the survival curve. Data come from a proportional
hazards Weibull model with exponential censoring; the truth follows from the
model in closed form.

```{r, eval = has_survival}
surv_study <- sim_study("survival_horizon",
  scenarios = sim_scenarios(n = c(100L, 400L), censoring = c(0.1, 0.3)),
  generate = function(scenario, context) {
    a <- rbinom(scenario$n, 1, 0.5)
    d <- sim_rweibull_ph(lp = -0.5 * a, lambda = 0.2, shape = 1.3,
                         censoring_rate = scenario$censoring, horizon = 5)
    d$a <- a
    # the uncensored event time is protected information
    sim_data(d[setdiff(names(d), "event_time")], meta = list(event_time = d$event_time))
  },
  estimands = list(sim_estimand("risk2", effect = "marginal", scale = "risk",
    horizon = 2, population = "treated arm",
    truth = sim_truth_exact(function(scenario) 1 - exp(-0.2 * 2^1.3 * exp(-0.5))))),
  methods = list(
    km = sim_method(function(data) {
      f <- survival::survfit(survival::Surv(time, status) ~ 1, data = data[data$a == 1, ])
      s <- summary(f, times = 2, extend = TRUE)
      sim_estimate("risk2", 1 - s$surv, se = s$std.err,
                   lower = 1 - s$upper, upper = 1 - s$lower, level = 0.95)
    }, packages = "survival"),
    naive = function(data) {
      # treats censored before 2 as event free: biased downwards
      d <- data[data$a == 1, ]
      p <- mean(d$status == 1 & d$time <= 2)
      se <- sqrt(p * (1 - p) / nrow(d))
      sim_estimate("risk2", p, se = se, lower = p - 1.96 * se, upper = p + 1.96 * se,
                   level = 0.95)
    }),
  measures = c("bias", "coverage"))
srun <- sim_run(surv_study, replications = 150, seed = 3,
                path = file.path(tempdir(), "survival"))
ss <- as.data.frame(sim_summarise(srun))
ss[ss$measure %in% c("bias", "coverage"),
   c("scenario_id", "method", "measure", "value", "mcse")]
```

The naive proportion ignores censoring and its bias grows with the
censoring rate; the Kaplan-Meier estimate is close to unbiased.

## Missing data and information boundaries

Outcomes are missing at random given a covariate. Complete case analysis
of the outcome mean is biased; inverse probability weighting with the
true missingness model is not. The study's generator knows the
missingness probabilities; the method must not. Methods only see the
scenario fields they declare, and data set level information from
`sim_data(meta = ...)` reaches only methods declared as oracles.

```{r}
missing_study <- sim_study("missing",
  scenarios = sim_scenarios(n = 300L, strength = c(0.5, 1.5)),
  generate = function(scenario, context) {
    x <- rnorm(scenario$n)
    y <- 1 + x + rnorm(scenario$n)
    d <- sim_add_missing(data.frame(x, y), "y", prop = 0.3, mechanism = "MAR",
                         predictors = "x", weights = scenario$strength)
    sim_data(d, meta = list(full_mean = mean(y)))
  },
  estimands = list(sim_estimand("mean_y", population = "all units",
                                truth = sim_truth_exact(function(scenario) 1))),
  methods = list(
    complete_case = function(data) {
      d <- data$y[!is.na(data$y)]
      sim_estimate("mean_y", mean(d), se = sd(d) / sqrt(length(d)))
    },
    ipw = function(data) {
      r <- !is.na(data$y)
      ps <- fitted(glm(r ~ x, binomial, data = data))
      sim_estimate("mean_y", sum(data$y[r] / ps[r]) / sum(1 / ps[r]))
    },
    regression = function(data) {
      f <- lm(y ~ x, data)
      sim_estimate("mean_y", mean(predict(f, newdata = data)))
    }),
  measures = c("bias", "empse", "rmse"))
mrun <- sim_run(missing_study, replications = 150, seed = 4,
                path = file.path(tempdir(), "missing"))
ms <- as.data.frame(sim_summarise(mrun))
ms[ms$measure == "bias", c("scenario_id", "method", "value", "mcse")]
```

## Meta-analysis: heterogeneity estimators

The `metafor` package fits random effects meta-analyses with several
estimators of the between-study variance. With few studies, the
DerSimonian-Laird interval is known to undercover; the Hartung-Knapp
adjustment is designed to fix that. With only 150 replications, coverage
differences of a few percentage points are within Monte Carlo error, as
the MCSE column shows; a real comparison would need several thousand.

```{r, eval = has_metafor}
meta_study <- sim_study("meta",
  scenarios = sim_scenarios(k = c(5L, 20L), tau = c(0.1, 0.4)),
  generate = function(scenario, context) {
    vi <- runif(scenario$k, 0.02, 0.2)
    yi <- rnorm(scenario$k, 0.2 + rnorm(scenario$k, 0, scenario$tau), sqrt(vi))
    data.frame(yi, vi)
  },
  estimands = list(sim_estimand("mu", effect = "marginal",
                                truth = sim_truth_exact(function(scenario) 0.2))),
  methods = list(
    dl = sim_method(function(data) {
      f <- metafor::rma(yi, vi, data = data, method = "DL")
      sim_estimate("mu", f$b[1], se = f$se, lower = f$ci.lb, upper = f$ci.ub, level = 0.95)
    }, packages = "metafor"),
    reml_hk = sim_method(function(data) {
      f <- metafor::rma(yi, vi, data = data, method = "REML", test = "knha")
      sim_estimate("mu", f$b[1], se = f$se, lower = f$ci.lb, upper = f$ci.ub,
                   level = 0.95)
    }, packages = "metafor")),
  measures = c("bias", "coverage", "width"))
mrun2 <- sim_run(meta_study, replications = 150, seed = 5,
                 path = file.path(tempdir(), "meta"))
m2 <- as.data.frame(sim_summarise(mrun2))
m2[m2$measure == "coverage", c("scenario_id", "method", "value", "mcse")]
```

REML can fail to converge with few studies; such failures are recorded
with their messages and appear in the failure table rather than
disappearing from the results.

## Noncompliance: intention to treat and the complier average causal effect

In a randomized trial with one-sided noncompliance, the intention to treat
(ITT) effect and the complier average causal effect (CACE) are different
estimands. With a constant treatment effect `delta` among those treated and
a proportion `pc` of compliers, the ITT effect is `pc * delta` and the CACE
is `delta`. Here compliance depends on an unmeasured prognostic variable `u`,
so an as-treated comparison confounds treatment with prognosis. Each method
declares the estimand it targets, and bias is computed against that
estimand only; comparing the bias of the ITT analysis with that of the
instrumental variable estimator would compare answers to different
questions.

```{r}
cace_study <- sim_study("noncompliance",
  scenarios = sim_scenarios(n = 400L, pc = c(0.5, 0.8), delta = 1),
  generate = function(scenario, context) {
    z <- rbinom(scenario$n, 1, 0.5)
    u <- rnorm(scenario$n)
    complier <- u > qnorm(1 - scenario$pc)
    d <- z * complier
    y <- 1 + u + scenario$delta * d + rnorm(scenario$n)
    data.frame(z, d, y)
  },
  estimands = list(
    sim_estimand("itt", effect = "marginal", population = "randomized",
                 truth = sim_truth_exact(function(scenario) scenario$pc * scenario$delta)),
    sim_estimand("cace", effect = "marginal", population = "compliers",
                 truth = sim_truth_exact(function(scenario) scenario$delta))),
  methods = list(
    itt = sim_method(function(data) {
      sim_estimate("itt", mean(data$y[data$z == 1]) - mean(data$y[data$z == 0]))
    }, estimands = "itt"),
    iv = sim_method(function(data) {
      itt_y <- mean(data$y[data$z == 1]) - mean(data$y[data$z == 0])
      itt_d <- mean(data$d[data$z == 1]) - mean(data$d[data$z == 0])
      sim_estimate("cace", itt_y / itt_d)
    }, estimands = "cace"),
    as_treated = sim_method(function(data) {
      sim_estimate("cace", mean(data$y[data$d == 1]) - mean(data$y[data$d == 0]))
    }, estimands = "cace")),
  measures = c("bias", "empse"))
crun <- sim_run(cace_study, replications = 200, seed = 21,
                path = file.path(tempdir(), "cace"))
cs <- as.data.frame(sim_summarise(crun))
cs[cs$measure == "bias", c("scenario_id", "method", "estimand", "value", "mcse")]
```

The ITT and instrumental variable estimators are unbiased for their own
estimands; the as-treated comparison is biased for the CACE because the
treated group holds only compliers, who have higher `u`.
